findings.problem: The voice changes four to the power X into base two but never says why. A student does not learn that the reason is so that every term is a power of the same number, two.
findings.fix: Add one sentence before 'Four is two squared', such as 'The other term is a power of two, so write four as a power of two too, then every term uses base two'. Light the 2^x in line 0 as it is named.

findings.problem: 'A quadratic in disguise' is said with no reason. A student is not told why letting A equal two to the power X helps: the equation holds only 2^x and its square, so it becomes a quadratic in A.
findings.fix: Say 'The equation has two to the power X, and two to the power X squared, so it is a quadratic in two to the power X'. Light the (2^x)^2 in line 3 and the 2^x in line 2 as each is named, before writing 'Let a = 2^x'.

findings.problem: Line 6 appears with nothing lit, so a student does not see that 2^{2x} became a² and 3(2^x) became 3a in the equation on line 2.
findings.fix: On 'the equation becomes', light {r1} and {r2a, r2x, r2b} in line 2. Then write line 6 with a² and 3a in the same colours.

findings.problem: 'The powers match, so X equals one' does not say why matching powers is allowed. The reason is that both sides now have the same base, two.
findings.fix: Say 'Both sides have base two, so the powers are equal: X equals one'. Add a note 'same base ⇒ compare powers' under {x1}.
